status: UNAPPROVED SEED. Not clinically validated. Requires review and sign-off by the Head of Clinical Pharmacy and the Allergy Committee before any deployment where it can gate a real order.
rationale: StewardMD has no allergy cross-reactivity data anywhere (surveyed 2026-09-04). The deterministic Allergy Shield in wardsynq-safety.js is inert without class membership and cross-reactivity, so this file exists to make the mechanism testable and to give pharmacy something concrete to correct. Membership lists are deliberately short and common-drug-only rather than exhaustive: a short list that is right is safer than a long list that is half wrong, because a wrong class assignment silently blocks or silently permits.
sources: Beta-lactam cross-reactivity figures reflect the modern side-chain-based understanding rather than the historical 10 percent penicillin-to-cephalosporin figure, which originated from studies using cephalosporins contaminated with penicillin and is now regarded as a substantial overestimate.
Cross-reactivity here is driven primarily by shared R1 side chains, not by the beta-lactam ring itself.
Every likelihood value below needs local verification against the site's own formulary and allergy service before sign-off.

2026-09-07, cephalosporin membership audit: the 10 cephalosporins added to `cephalosporins` on this date were not chosen from memory. Each is tagged `epc:cephalosporin_antibacterial` by data/interaction-rules.json itself (openFDA/RxNorm-derived), and each was absent from this list while resolving perfectly in the pack - so an order for one belonged to no allergy class and produced no cross-reactivity warning at all. Note cefotetan and cefoxitin are strictly cephamycins; they are tagged as cephalosporins by the source data and are handled as such for allergy purposes, which pharmacy should confirm. NOTHING was added to cephalosporins_r1_aminopenicillin_like: R1 side-chain similarity is a specific clinical property and that list stays exactly as pharmacy curated it.

crossReactivity.note: Shared R1 side chain with aminopenicillins. This is the highest-risk beta-lactam crossing and the one worth acting on.
Approximately 1 to 2 percent where side chains differ. The historical 10 percent figure is now considered a substantial overestimate. Do not reflexively withhold a cephalosporin on this basis alone.
Under 1 percent. A carbapenem is usually acceptable in penicillin allergy after assessment.
Aztreonam is generally safe in penicillin allergy. Note separately that aztreonam shares an R1 side chain with ceftazidime, so caution applies to that specific pair rather than to penicillins.

Recorded deliberately as NONE. Cross-reactivity between sulfonamide antibiotics and non-antibiotic sulfonamides such as furosemide or hydrochlorothiazide is a persistent misconception; encoding it explicitly stops a well-meaning reviewer from adding it later.
Cross-reactivity among aromatic anticonvulsants is high, particularly for severe cutaneous reactions. Treat a documented severe reaction to one as applying to the group.
